sections.heading: Noticing how easily I drift
sections.text:
Lord, when people around me turn away from you and stop listening to your call, I do not want to pretend I am untouched by it. In seasons when unbelief feels normal and faithfulness feels strange, my own heart can slide with the world more than I want to admit.

Thank you for the mercy that does not leave me asleep in danger. Thank you for warning me, waking me up, and calling me to keep holding on to you.
theological_themes: The world’s unbelief can influence believers toward spiritual drift.
God’s grace warns his people and calls them to perseverance.
Self-awareness before God is itself a mercy.

scripture_references.connection: This passage warns believers against an unbelieving heart that falls away and calls them to persevere together in faith. It supports the prayer’s concern that surrounding unbelief can harden the heart and that God’s warning is a gift.

Paul calls Christians not to be conformed to the pattern of the present age but to be transformed by God. This speaks directly to the danger of drifting with the world rather than remaining faithful to God.

sections.heading: Coming back with nothing to offer
sections.text:
I praise you that when I have turned aside, I do not have to wait until I can make myself impressive before I come home. I can return to you now. You receive sinners who have nothing to bring except need, confession, and empty hands.

All my past wanderings do not make your mercy smaller. You welcome me because of your grace, not because I have managed to repair myself.
theological_themes: Repentance is immediate return to God, not self-improvement first.
God receives the undeserving by grace.
Forgiveness rests on God’s mercy, not human merit.

scripture_references.connection: In Jesus’ parable, the father receives the returning son before the son can offer any repayment or proof of worthiness. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that a backslider may return with empty hands and be welcomed by grace.
John teaches that confession of sin is met by God’s faithful forgiveness and cleansing. This supports the prayer’s movement from backsliding to immediate return and pardon.

sections.heading: Confessing where I have been living wrong
sections.text:
This is my own case, Father. Lately I have felt spiritually poor and dull. I have not seen your grace clearly. My soul has been troubled, and part of the trouble is that I have not come as I should to the cleansing you have provided.

I have tried too hard to produce spiritual life, a quiet conscience, and real holiness by my own effort. I have acted as if I could make myself alive, cleanse myself, and carry myself forward without depending on you.
theological_themes: Spiritual poverty and dullness come when grace is not rightly apprehended.
Cleansing from sin is found in God’s provision, not self-effort.
Sanctification cannot be produced in self-reliance.

scripture_references.connection: Zechariah speaks of a fountain opened for cleansing from sin and uncleanness. The original prayer’s image of coming to the fountain that purges sin is naturally illuminated by this promise of God-provided cleansing.

Paul rebukes believers for trying to continue by the flesh after beginning by the Spirit. This directly supports the confession that spiritual life and holiness cannot be maintained by self-powered religion.

Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This grounds the prayer’s admission that peace, fruitfulness, and holiness must come from dependence on Christ rather than personal strength.

sections.heading: Asking you to bring me back by your power and love
sections.text:
Please show me again the strength of your arm. Help me believe that you can do far more in me than I can ask for or even imagine.

Even when I backslide, do not let me go. Draw me back with your steady, everlasting love. Meet me with grace in the wilderness places where I have become weak and lost. Bring me out leaning on Christ, my beloved Savior.

Lead me with him beside living water, on a straight road, where you keep my feet from stumbling.
theological_themes: God’s power is sufficient to restore the drifting believer.
God’s covenant love holds and draws back his people.
Christ is the one on whom the believer leans in weakness.
God can guide, refresh, and preserve his people through spiritual wilderness.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God as able to do far more abundantly than believers ask or think. This supports the request for renewed faith in God’s power to restore and strengthen beyond the limits of the believer’s imagination.
God speaks of loving his people with everlasting love and continuing faithfulness. This grounds the prayer’s confidence that divine love draws the backslider back rather than abandoning him.
The image of coming up from the wilderness leaning on the beloved comes from this verse. In Christian devotional use, it fittingly expresses dependence on Christ through weakness and restoration.
God promises to lead his people by brooks of water in a straight path where they will not stumble. This supports the prayer’s request for God to guide, refresh, and preserve the returning believer.

sections.heading: Keeping me faithful by free grace
sections.text:
Keep me serious about sin, tender toward you, and faithful in ordinary obedience. Do not let me trust my own resolve as if it were strong enough.

Teach me to rest on your free grace for the help I need, for acceptance before you, and for peace in my conscience. Hold me close, and keep me walking with you.
theological_themes: The believer needs ongoing grace for faithfulness and perseverance.
Acceptance before God rests on grace, not personal performance.
Peace of conscience comes from God’s saving work, not self-confidence.

scripture_references.connection: Because of Christ, believers are invited to draw near to receive mercy and grace for need. This supports the prayer’s dependence on free grace for help rather than self-reliance.
Paul connects justification by faith with peace with God and access into grace. This grounds the prayer’s longing for acceptance and peace of conscience in God’s grace through Christ.
Jude ends by praising God as the one able to keep his people from stumbling and present them blameless. This supports the request that God himself preserve the believer in faithfulness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The opening language about unbelievers being so forsaken by God that he calls them no more reflects a strong Puritan sense of judicial hardening and divine abandonment. Because Christians differ on how to articulate reprobation and the limits of God’s saving call, the adaptation renders the idea more pastorally but still seriously as people turning away and no longer listening to God’s call, without making a universal claim about any identifiable person’s final state.

The original assumes that in times of general apostasy even true believers may backslide ‘in some measure with the world.’ This has been preserved as a confession of vulnerability to cultural unbelief, not as an excuse or inevitability.
significant_interpretive_choices: The phrase ‘fountain that purges away all sin’ was interpreted as God’s provision of cleansing through Christ, with Zechariah 13:1 used as the biblical background rather than introducing new sacramental language.

The request to be brought out of the wilderness ‘leaning on the arm of my Beloved’ was retained as dependence on Christ, while noting that the wording echoes Song of Solomon 8:5 in a traditional Christian devotional reading.
‘Show me the arm of all might’ was rendered as a request to see and trust God’s restoring power, rather than as a demand for dramatic experience.
